# Laws of UX

The Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski) that the guideposts in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) do not already apply. Each entry gives the law and what it means for a design.

## Perception and grouping

- **Aesthetic-usability effect.** Users think an attractive design is easier to use, and they tolerate small problems in it. Polish hides usability problems in testing too, so test with tasks.
- **Law of common region.** Items inside one clear boundary (a card, a panel) read as a group.
- **Law of proximity.** Items near each other read as a group. Spacing is the cheapest way to group.
- **Law of similarity.** Items that look the same read as related. Make items that act differently look different.
- **Law of uniform connectedness.** Items joined by a line or a shared frame read as more related than items that are only near.
- **Law of Prägnanz.** People see complex shapes as the simplest possible form. Use simple, clear shapes.
- **Von Restorff effect.** The one item that differs is the one users remember. Use this only for the most important item. When everything is emphasized, nothing is.

## Memory and attention

- **Miller's Law.** Working memory holds about 7 (±2) items. Chunk content; do not use the number as a hard limit on menu items.
- **Serial position effect.** Users remember the first and last items in a list best. Put the most important items at the start and end.
- **Selective attention.** Users notice only what relates to their goal, and they ignore what looks like an advertisement (banner blindness). Put important information where the user's task already looks.
- **Zeigarnik effect.** Users remember unfinished tasks. Show clear progress for incomplete work, so the user can continue.
- **Peak-end rule.** Users judge an experience by its best or worst moment and by its end. Make the peak and the end good, for example a clear success state.
- **Goal-gradient effect.** Users move faster as they get closer to a goal. Show progress, and give a head start when you can.

## Models and complexity

- **Mental model.** Users have a model of how the system works, built from other products. Match it, or teach the new model explicitly.
- **Paradox of the active user.** Users start to use software immediately and do not read manuals. Put guidance in context, where the user needs it.
- **Tesler's Law.** Every system has some complexity that you cannot remove. Move it from the user to the system where you can (good defaults, inferred values).
- **Occam's razor.** Of two designs that work equally well, choose the one with fewer parts.
- **Pareto principle.** About 80% of use comes from about 20% of features. Make that 20% excellent and easy to reach.
- **Postel's Law.** Accept input liberally (formats, spacing, case), and give output strictly and consistently.
- **Parkinson's Law.** A task takes all the time it is given. Make tasks shorter than users expect, for example with autofill.
- **Cognitive bias.** Users decide with shortcuts that bias them. Design defaults and framing honestly.
